subject: Critical Thinking
title: Karl Popper: Science Advances by Trying to Be Wrong
description: One-minute skill: Karl Popper: Science Advances by Trying to Be Wrong.

hook.text: What makes something 'scientific'? Not proof. Karl Popper said: science is defined by what COULD prove it wrong.

buildup.text: Popper's falsifiability criterion: a theory is scientific only if it makes predictions that could, in principle, be.

discovery.text: Einstein's relativity: it predicted light bending around the sun.

twist.text: Freudian psychology & Marxist history explain EVERYTHING – no outcome could falsify them.

climax.text: The lesson for all thinking: if nothing could change your mind, your belief isn't based on evidence.

punchline.text: Real confidence says: 'Here's what would prove me wrong.' False confidence.

quiz.question: According to Popper, what makes a theory scientific?
options: It makes predictions that could, in principle, be shown to be false

details.summary: Karl Popper argued that science advances not by proving theories true but by trying to prove them false. A theory that cannot be falsified is not scientific. This falsificationist criterion became the standard for distinguishing science from pseudoscience.
details.whyItMatters: Popper's insight changed how scientists think about their own work and gave the public a clear standard for evaluating whether a claim is genuinely scientific.
takeaways: Science progresses through falsification, not verification
The best theories are the most testable ones

faq.question: What is the difference between verification and falsification in Popper's framework?
faq.answer: Verification tries to prove a theory true, which is logically impossible for universal claims. Falsification tries to prove a theory wrong, which requires only one counterexample. Popper argued science should pursue falsification because it is logically decisive.

faq.question: What prompted Popper to develop his falsification criterion?
faq.answer: Popper noticed that theories like Marxism and psychoanalysis could explain any observation, which made them seem powerful but actually made them untestable. Einstein's theory, by contrast, made risky predictions that could be proven wrong.
